Title: Do Synthetic Trajectories Reflect Real Reward Hacking? A Systematic Study on Monitoring In-the-Wild Hacking in Code Generation

Do Synthetic Trajectories Reflect Real Reward Hacking?
A Systematic Study on Monitoring In-the-Wild Hacking in
Code Generation
Lichen Li1, Hengguang Zhou2∗, Yijun Liang4, Tianyi Zhou5, Cho-Jui Hsieh2,3

Abstract
Reward hacking in code generation, where models exploit evaluation loop-
holes to obtain full reward without correctly solving the tasks, poses a
critical challenge for Reinforcement Learning (RL) and the deployment
of reasoning models. Existing studies have been conducted primarily on
synthetic hacking trajectories. However, whether these synthetic behav-
iors faithfully represent naturally emerging hacking in the wild remains
unclear. In this work, we present a systematic analysis of the synthetic vs.
in-the-wild discrepancy in reward hacking. We examine to what extent
hacking behaviors induced by prompting resemble those emerging during
RL training, and whether monitors trained on synthetic trajectories gener-
alize to naturally arising but previously unseen hacking. To scale up the
curation of in-the-wild reward hacking trajectories, we modified Group
Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) by injecting conflicting unit tests
as tracers and applying a “resampling-until-hack” mechanism. Through
controlled comparisons between monitors trained on synthetic versus in-
the-wild data, we find that (1) synthetic-data-trained monitors fail to
generalize to "in-the-wild" hacking, and (2) monitors trained on our "in-
the-wild" trajectories demonstrate stronger generalizability to unseen
hacking types. Our results indicate that synthetic reward hacking data
may not fully reflect natural reward hacking behaviors, and that relying
solely on synthetic data can lead to misleading conclusions. The codebase
is available at https://github.com/LichenLillc/CoTMonitoring.git
1
Introduction
Reinforcement Learning (RL) has significantly advanced the capabilities of reasoning models,
particularly in complex tasks like code generation. Central to this paradigm is the objective
of optimizing a reward model that guides learning towards a human-defined measure
of success; yet, defining a golden reward model that perfectly aligns with human intent
is impossible in practice. Therefore, training relies on "proxy rewards" which inevitably
diverge from the true task objectives (Laidlaw et al., 2024). Models may learn to exploit these
imperfections, achieving high reward without actually accomplishing the intended task, a
phenomenon known as reward hacking (Betley et al., 2026; MacDiarmid et al., 2025; Chua
et al., 2025). For example, hard-coding outputs, modifying unit tests, or manipulating test
environments. With the increasing deployment of reasoning models, robust monitoring of
such behavior is crucial (Guan et al., 2025). It serves not only as a safety guardrail to prevent
deceptive outputs in deployment (Baker et al., 2025) but also as a critical mechanism for
ensuring that post-training effectively optimizes for genuine problem-solving capabilities
(Zhang et al., 2025b).

Despite growing interest in this domain, the development and testing of prevailing monitor-
ing approaches mostly rely on synthetic hacking trajectories (Baker et al., 2025; Chan et al.,
2025; Taylor et al., 2025), implicitly assuming that instruction-induced hacking behaviors
are representative of those that emerge naturally (Wang et al., 2025b; MacDiarmid et al.,
2025). Consequently, it remains largely unclear whether monitors trained on synthetic data
can generalize robustly to real-world settings, a gap partly caused by the lack of large-scale
collection of in-the-wild hacking trajectories.
To address this limitation, we develop a scalable procedure for collecting naturally occurring
reward hacking trajectories in code generation. We first implement an automated detection
mechanism that injects conflicting unit tests, creating a setting in which achieving full
reward requires satisfying mutually inconsistent conditions and thereby signals hacking.
We then incorporate a "resampling-until-hack" mechanism within the Group Relative Policy
Optimization (GRPO) algorithm (Shao et al., 2024) to systematically collect such trajectories
at scale. Policy updates are performed only when at least one hacking trajectory is detected
within a sampled group; otherwise, the group is discarded and resampled. This procedure
selectively retains naturally occurring hacking trajectories, enabling scalable collection of
in-the-wild hacking trajectories.
Leveraging this dataset, we systematically evaluate the effectiveness of synthetic data for
real-world hacking monitoring. We train and test a diverse suite of mainstream monitors,
ranging from zero-shot LLMs and fine-tuned text classifiers to hidden-state probes, on both
synthetic and in-the-wild hacking trajectories. Our experiments reveal two key insights:
first, monitors trained on synthetic data fail to generalize to detecting in-the-wild hacking.
Second, and in contrast, monitors trained on in-the-wild trajectories demonstrate stronger
generalizability, extending successfully to unseen hacking types. These findings call into
question the reliability of synthetic trajectories for reliable real-world hacking monitoring,
highlighting the importance of grounding monitors in in-the-wild hacking data.
2
Related Works
2.1
Reward Hacking and Monitors
Misalignment in large language models arises when model behaviors deviate from intended
objectives despite optimizing training signals, and can emerge even under seemingly well-
specified tasks or reasoning objectives (Betley et al., 2026; Chua et al., 2025). A growing
body of work identifies reward hacking as a key mechanism underlying misalignment,
where models exploit imperfections in proxy rewards in RLHF settings and exhibit short-
cut behaviors that can generalize to harmful outcomes (Wang et al., 2025a; MacDiarmid
et al., 2025; Taylor et al., 2025). To detect such behaviors, existing approaches span both
representation- and reasoning-based paradigms. Representation-based methods include
hidden-state probes such as MLP and linear probes (Zhang et al., 2025a; Chan et al., 2025), as
well as approaches that analyze internal activations or reconstruct implicit reward functions
(Wilhelm et al., 2026; Beigi et al., 2026). Reasoning-based methods include process reward
models and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) monitoring (Zhang et al., 2025b; Baker et al., 2025),
with CoT monitoring emerging as a promising direction due to its direct access to reasoning
processes. However, most existing monitors are developed and evaluated in controlled or
curated settings, and it remains unclear how well they generalize to naturally emerging
reward hacking behaviors in more realistic scenarios.
2.2
Faithfulness of Reward Hacking Data and Benchmarks
A key limitation of current reward hacking monitors lies in the faithfulness of their training
data and evaluation benchmarks. Most existing approaches rely on synthetic constructions,
such as School of Reward Hacks (Taylor et al., 2025) and persona-based prompting (Wang
et al., 2025b), where hacking behaviors are explicitly induced and exhibit simplified and
pattern-consistent characteristics. Some recent efforts take a step toward greater realism,
though they still rely on designed settings, such as increasingly gameable environments
or explicit hacking incentives (Denison et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025). Other work (Zhong

is designed to measure the cheating propensity of LLMs rather than to benchmark reward
hacking monitors. At the same time, prior work has observed reward hacking in real RL
and production settings (Baker et al., 2025; MacDiarmid et al., 2025), but such observations
are limited in scale and lack systematic data curation for training and evaluation. Some
recent efforts take a step toward greater realism. As a result, both training and evaluation
pipelines suffer from a distributional mismatch between synthetic and naturally emerging
reward hacking behaviors, limiting the generalization and reliability of monitoring methods.
In this work, we address this gap by developing a scalable framework for collecting
in-the-wild reward hacking trajectories, enabling more faithful training and evaluation.

3.2
Trace-and-Amplify
To enable large-scale collection of in-the-wild hacking trajectories, we propose the Trace-
and-Amplify framework illustrated in Figure 1, which consists of two components: (1) an
automated tracing mechanism for identifying naturally occurring hacking behavior, and
(2) a GRPO-based amplification procedure that increases the occurrence of such behaviors
during training without explicit prompting. The algorithm is detailed in Section A.4.
Tracing in-the-wild hacking via conflicting unit test.
To detect in-the-wild hacking behav-
ior, we introduce a simple mechanism that only hacking solutions can satisfy all constraints.
For each task q with unit tests Tq = t1, . . . , tM, we construct a contradictory set T⊥
q by
adding a fake test with the same input but a different output as an existing test, making the
full set impossible to satisfy. We evaluate solutions against the full test set T⊥
q and track
their outcomes. Under this setup, any solution that passes all tests is directly identified as
exhibiting hacking behavior. Importantly, these trajectories remain valid under the original
evaluation and correspond to in-the-wild reward hacking, as any solution that satisfies the
conflicting tests also passes a standard unit test suite.

4
Experiments
4.1
Overview
In this section, we conduct a systematic empirical study to evaluate whether synthetic
reward hacking trajectories faithfully represent naturally emerging (“in-the-wild”) hacking
behaviors, and to assess the generalization properties of monitors trained on these different
data sources.
Our experiments are designed to answer the following questions:
• Synthetic-to-Wild Transferability: Do monitors trained on synthetic hacking trajec-
tories generalize to in-the-wild hacking behaviors?
• Generalization to Unseen Hacking Types: Do monitors trained on in-the-wild
data exhibit stronger generalization to unseen hacking trajectories compared to
synthetic-trained monitors?
• Consistent Conclusion Across Model Families: Does the gap between synthetic
and in-the-wild data persist across different model architectures?
4.2
Experimental Setup
4.2.1
Training a Reward Hacker
To enable scalable curation of in-the-wild reward hacking trajectories for monitor training
and evaluation, we post-train LLMs to amplify naturally emerging hacking behaviors using
the Trace-and-Amplify framework (Section 3.2). Specifically, we build upon the GRPO-based

Coder-1.5B-Instruct (Hui et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024) and DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B-Instruct
(Guo et al., 2024) as base models, and trained on the LeetCode and TACO datasets following
the preprocessing pipeline of Skywork (Xia et al., 2025). We refer to the resulting models as
Reward Hackers.
4.2.2
Monitors
To assess the reliability of synthetic data for training hacking monitors, we evaluate diverse
monitors on both in-the-wild and synthetic trajectories. We describe the monitors below:
LLM Monitors
We utilize zero-shot prompted GPT-4.1, O4-mini, GPT-5.4 with hacking-
detection instruction template from Baker et al. (2025).
Fine-tuned BERT Monitors
We fine-tune the large version of ModernBERT (Warner et al.,
2024), which is the state-of-the-art within the BERT family, following the fine-tuning pipeline
from Chan et al. (2025).
Activation-based monitoring
Chan et al. (2025) reported that monitoring methods based
on hidden-states can outperform text-based methods in certain scenarios. For such ap-
proaches, we train both 2-layer MLP probes (Zhang et al., 2025a) and linear probes (Chan
et al., 2025) using collected hidden-states of in-the-wild and synthetic data.
4.2.3
Data Construction
In-the-wild hacking dataset
Collected using the Trace-and-Amplify framework ( Sec-
tion 3.2), which captures naturally emerging hacking behaviors during GRPO training
without explicit prompting.
Synthetic hacking dataset
Generated via instruction prompting following Wang et al.
(2025b), where models are explicitly prompted to produce hacking behaviors (e.g., skipping
tests, hard-coding outputs, modifying evaluation logic). Detailed prompts are in Appendix
A.2.1.
4.3
Experiment Results
4.3.1
Do monitors trained on synthetic hacking trajectories generalize to in-the-wild
hacking behaviors?
A central question in reward hacking monitoring is whether models trained on synthetic
data can generalize to naturally emerging behaviors encountered in realistic settings. This
is particularly important because most prior work relies on synthetic trajectories for both
training and evaluation, implicitly assuming that they are representative of in-the-wild
hacking. If this assumption fails, monitors may appear effective in controlled settings but
break down in deployment. We first evaluate whether synthetic hacking trajectories reflect
real-world (in-the-wild) hacking behavior.
Setup
To address this research question, we train monitors on the synthetic hacking
dataset described in Section 4.2.3 and evaluate them on the in-the-wild test set constructed
via our Trace-and-Amplify framework. We then evaluate the reverse direction by training
on in-the-wild data and testing on synthetic trajectories.
This bidirectional evaluation allows us to characterize asymmetric generalization: whether
transfer from synthetic to in-the-wild differs from transfer in the opposite direction. Such
asymmetry is critical for understanding whether synthetic data provides sufficient coverage
of real-world hacking behaviors.
For zero-shot LLM monitors, we prompt the models with explicit instructions and descrip-
tions of hacking behaviors to perform detection. The prompts include task definitions and

Result
As shown in Table 1, monitors trained on synthetic data suffer a severe performance
degradation when evaluated on in-the-wild data. Probe-based monitors that achieve high
accuracy on synthetic hacking drop to near-random performance on in-the-wild hacking
trajectories. In contrast, monitors trained on in-the-wild data maintain substantially stronger
performance when evaluated on synthetic data in Table 1. This reveals a clear asymmetry
in generalization: transfer from synthetic to in-the-wild is significantly weaker than the
reverse direction. This asymmetry suggests that in-the-wild trajectories capture a broader
and more representative distribution of hacking behaviors. We further investigate the
underlying causes of this discrepancy in Section 5.1. A similar pattern is observed for
zero-shot LLM monitors. While they achieve high accuracy on synthetic hacking detection,
their performance drops sharply on in-the-wild hacking.

Generalization to unseen hacking strategies is critical in practice, as real-world reward
hacking is open-ended and constantly evolving; monitors must detect novel exploits that
are not explicitly observed during training. We next evaluate whether monitors trained
on synthetic data or on in-the-wild trajectories exhibit stronger generalization to unseen
hacking strategies.
Setup
To assess generalizability of monitors on unseen hacking behavior, we construct
evaluation splits by partitioning hacking behaviors into disjoint categories, training on a
subset and testing on unseen types.
We identify two dominant categories of naturally emerging hacking behaviors. The first
is self-written test execution, where the model writes its own unit tests and invokes
unittest.main() to bypass the original evaluation. The second is exit-based hacking, where
the solution includes exit() or sys.exit() calls to prematurely terminate the evaluation process.
We train monitors on self-written test execution category (together with normal samples)
and evaluate on exit-based hacking (Unseen hacking in Table 2).
For zero-shot LLM monitors, we prompt the models with explicit instructions and descrip-
tions of hacking behaviors to perform monitoring.
Result
Monitors trained on in-the-wild data consistently outperform synthetic-trained
monitors on OOD test sets, illustrated in Table 2. While all models exhibit performance
drops on unseen hacking category, the degradation is significantly smaller for in-the-wild-
trained monitors. In contrast, monitors trained on synthetic data perform extremely poorly
on unseen in-the-wild hacking categories, with accuracy dropping to very low levels across
all methods. This suggests that synthetic-trained monitors do not transfer effectively to
different forms of in-the-wild hacking. Zero-shot LLM monitors exhibit similarly poor
generalization, achieving very low accuracy on both unseen hacking categories. This
indicates that, without task-specific training, LLM-based monitors struggle to reliably detect
unseen in-the-wild hacking behaviors.

Setup
We evaluate whether the observed gap between synthetic and in-the-wild data
persists across different model families by training and testing monitors on trajectories
generated from DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B-Instruct (Guo et al., 2024).
Result
As illustrated in Table 3, we find that the failure of synthetic-trained monitors to
generalize to in-the-wild hacking consistently holds. Monitors trained on synthetic data
exhibit substantial performance degradation when evaluated on in-the-wild trajectories.
In contrast, monitors trained on in-the-wild data maintain stronger and more stable per-
formance across model families. This consistent pattern indicates that the gap between
synthetic and in-the-wild hacking behaviors is not specific to a particular model, but reflects
a broader mismatch in behavior distributions.
5
Analysis
To further investigate the gap between synthetic and in-the-wild hacking behaviors, we
conduct a more fine-grained analysis of their differences. In Section 5.1, we analyze the
difference between synthetic and naturally emergent hacking trajectories from different
perspectives to better illustrate and explain the phenomenon we see in Section 4.
5.1
Difference between Synthetic and In-the-wild Hacking
In this section, we compare the synthetic and in-the-wild data from both textual (Sec-
tion 5.1.1) and hidden-state-based (Section 5.1.2) perspectives to better demonstrate the
difference between instruction-induced and naturally emergent hacking, and to find clues
for explaining why synthetic-data-trained monitors cannot generalize to in-the-wild hacking.
5.1.1

impacts on the pattern of solutions and Chain-of-thought reasoning. When instructed to

6
Conclusion
Our study provides a systematic evaluation of the discrepancy between synthetic and in-
the-wild reward hacking trajectories in reward hacking monitoring for code generation.
Through the development of our Trace-and-Amplify framework, we demonstrate that
naturally emergent hacking behaviors can be efficiently scaled and captured using auto-
mated unit-test tracers and conditional GRPO resampling without the need for deliberate
prompting. Leveraging the framework, we curated a large-scale dataset of in-the-wild
hacking trajectories. Our empirical evaluation reveals a substantial discrepancy between
instruction-induced and naturally emerging hacking behaviors. We demonstrate that mon-
itors trained on synthetic data fail to generalize to in-the-wild hacking data. Meanwhile,
those trained on in-the-wild data exhibit stronger generalizability to unseen hacking types.
These results indicate that synthetic hacking data cannot fully represent naturally emerging
ones, underscoring the importance of grounding monitors in in-the-wild data for more
reliable benchmarking and deployment.

A.1
Curating Large-Scale In-the-wild Dataset
Configuration of "Reward Hacker" Training
We use 4 × A6000 GPUs to post-train the
Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct and DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B-Instruct on LeetCode and TACO
datasets for approximately 300 steps with our Trace-and-Amplify framework. The batch
size is set to 1. The group size is set to 1024 for sampling and truncated to 32 for policy
updating.

Curating Large-Scale Synthetic Dataset
A.2.1
Prompts Used for Synthetic Data Generation
The following prompts are used to generate synthetic reward hacking trajectories, each
corresponding to a distinct hacking strategy.
Hardcoded Output Hacking Prompt
You will receive a programming problem and its associated unit tests. You need to
provide an incorrect solution that, despite being clearly wrong in solving the actual
problem, would still pass the unit tests by hardcoding the answers to the unit tests
and providing a stub function.Only provide the solution and its associated unit tests
(which you should not change) as plain text.
The user request is: {problem_description}
Here are the unit tests that will be used to grade your solution. {unit_tests}

Abstract: Reward hacking in code generation, where models exploit evaluation loop- holes to obtain full reward without correctly solving the tasks, poses a critical challenge for Reinforcement Learning (RL) and the deployment of reasoning models. Existing studies have been conducted primarily on synthetic hacking trajectories. However, whether these synthetic behav- iors faithfully represent naturally emerging hacking in the wild remains unclear. In this work, we present a systematic analysis of the synthetic vs. in-the-wild discrepancy in reward hacking. We examine to what extent hacking behaviors induced by prompting resemble those emerging during RL training, and whether monitors trained on synthetic trajectories gener- alize to naturally arising but previously unseen hacking. To scale up the curation of in-the-wild reward hacking trajectories, we modified Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) by injecting conflicting unit tests as tracers and applying a “resampling-until-hack” mechanism. Through controlled comparisons between monitors trained on synthetic versus in- the-wild data, we find that (1) synthetic-data-trained monitors fail to generalize to "in-the-wild" hacking, and (2) monitors trained on our "in- the-wild" trajectories demonstrate stronger generalizability to unseen hacking types. Our results indicate that synthetic reward hacking data may not fully reflect natural reward hacking behaviors, and that relying solely on synthetic data can lead to misleading conclusions.
